subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Arabic Coffee Traditions
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Arabic Coffee Traditions.

hook.text: In Arab culture, coffee is a symbol of hospitality. Refusing a cup can be a serious insult.

buildup.text: Arabic coffee uses lightly roasted beans brewed with cardamom. It's served in small handleless cups.

discovery.text: The host always pours for guests first, filling cups only one-third full—a sign of frequent refills.

twist.text: Shaking your cup side to side signals you've had enough. Without that gesture, the host keeps pouring.

climax.text: UNESCO recognized Arabic coffee as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2015 for its deep social significance.

punchline.text: One-third cup, whole-hearted welcome. Coffee means hospitality.

quiz.question: How do you signal you've had enough Arabic coffee?
options: Shake the cup side to side

details.summary: Arabic coffee, known as qahwa, is a centuries-old tradition of serving lightly roasted coffee flavored with cardamom in small handleless cups called finjan. The host pours and serves from a dallah pot.
details.whyItMatters: Arabic coffee traditions show that coffee's oldest cultures treat it primarily as a vehicle for hospitality, not just a caffeinated drink.
takeaways: Arabic coffee uses lightly roasted beans flavored with cardamom
It is served from a dallah pot into small finjan cups
UNESCO recognizes it as intangible cultural heritage

faq.question: How is Arabic coffee different from espresso or drip coffee?
faq.answer: Arabic coffee uses very lightly roasted beans, often green-gold in color, which are ground with cardamom and sometimes saffron. The brew is thin and pale, not dark and concentrated. It tastes herbal, spicy, and light, nothing like Western coffee. The ritual of serving matters as much as the drink.

faq.question: What are the etiquette rules when drinking Arabic coffee?
faq.answer: Accept the cup with your right hand. Drink small sips, not large gulps. You will be offered multiple refills. To signal you have had enough, gently shake the cup from side to side. Refusing the first cup offered is considered rude. The host always serves the most honored guest first.
